Purpose  
To develop and evaluate a locally deployed multi-agent AI system for radiology report structuring and quality assurance (QA).

Materials and Methods  

Overview of Workflow  
This retrospective study assessed a two-stage AI pipeline for structuring and QA of radiology reports. The system first segmented reports into anatomical sections using a rule-based agent, then refined assignments and performed QA tasks using a local large language model (LLM) agent. Performance was evaluated by radiologist review of a stratified sample of reports.

Study Design and Data  
A total of 638 radiology reports from CT chest, abdomen, and pelvis exams, dictated by 15 board-certified radiologists at a single institution in 2023–2024, were included. Reports were randomly sampled for evaluation.

Multi-Agent AI Pipeline Architecture  

Rule-Based Agent  
The first agent used regular expressions (regex) to identify and segment sentences into standardized anatomical sections (e.g., lungs, liver, kidneys). Regex patterns such as `r"\b(lungs?|pulmonary)\b"` and `r"\b(liver|hepatic)\b"` were iteratively developed by reviewing 100 randomly selected local reports. Patterns were refined to maximize recall (target >95% of anatomical section headers correctly identified) and minimize false positives (target <5% incorrect assignments), as measured by manual review on a validation set of 50 reports. Performance was tracked by calculating the proportion of correctly and incorrectly assigned sentences per section.

LLM Agent and Prompt Engineering  
A 7B-parameter Llama-2 model, running on-premises, was used to resolve ambiguous assignments and perform semantic QA checks. The LLM was prompted with institution-specific instructions. For example, initial prompts were: “Assign the following sentence to the most appropriate anatomical section: [sentence].” Iterative prompt engineering included adding explicit lists of local section headers and reporting conventions, e.g., “Use the following section list: [list]. If uncertain, assign to ‘Other’.” Radiologist feedback was incorporated by having two radiologists review LLM outputs on 30 validation reports, rating accuracy and providing suggestions. Prompts were revised until >90% agreement with expert assignments was achieved on the validation set.

Agent Interaction and QA Tasks  
A controller script orchestrated the pipeline: the regex agent generated preliminary section assignments, which the LLM agent reviewed and refined. The LLM also performed three QA tasks using prompt-based logic:  
(a) Section mismatch: “Are there findings in the Findings section not reflected in the Impression, or vice versa?”  
(b) Gender-anatomy conflict: “Does the report mention anatomical findings inconsistent with the patient’s gender?”  
(c) Undocumented critical findings: “Is there mention of a critical finding, and if so, is communication documented?”  
Prompts for each task were validated by comparing LLM outputs to expert annotations on 50 reports, with error rates (false positives/negatives) tracked and prompts revised to minimize errors (<10% for each task).

Evaluation Design and Metrics  
A random subset of 45 reports was selected for radiologist evaluation, stratified to include 23 flagged and 22 unflagged reports, reflecting the overall flagged/unflagged ratio. The sample size was chosen to provide a 95% confidence interval of ±15% for the primary outcome (correct restructuring rate), based on pilot data showing 65–75% accuracy. This interval was considered acceptable for a feasibility study, but is a limitation for precise performance estimation. Two board-certified radiologists independently assessed:  
(1) Correctness of restructuring—defined as all sentences assigned to correct anatomical sections, with no omission or fabrication of clinically important information. Clinically important information was operationalized as findings that, if omitted or misassigned, could alter patient management (e.g., new or significant lesions, critical findings).  
(2) QA task performance—each flagged issue was rated as true/false positive/negative.  
(3) Omission or fabrication of clinically important information—examples included missing documentation of a pulmonary nodule or erroneous addition of a finding.  
Disagreements were resolved by consensus discussion; the frequency and nature of disagreements were recorded and categorized (e.g., section assignment, omission, fabrication).

System Requirements and Deployment  
The system was deployed on a workstation with dual NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPUs, 256 GB RAM, and Ubuntu 22.04. LLM inference averaged 2.5 seconds per report; regex processing was <0.1 seconds per report. This hardware exceeds typical clinical infrastructure, potentially limiting deployment. Possible solutions include model quantization or use of smaller models, but these were not explored here. The system operated as a standalone batch processor and was not integrated into clinical workflow.

Results  

Report Structuring  
The system structured the Findings sections of all 638 reports (22,270 sentences) into a predefined anatomical format, retaining original content. Of the 45 evaluated reports, both reviewers agreed that 31 (69%, 95% CI: 54–81%) were correctly restructured, 2 (4%, 95% CI: 0–13%) were incorrectly restructured, and 12 (27%, 95% CI: 15–41%) had reviewer disagreement. Correct restructuring required all sentences to be assigned to the correct anatomical section, with no omission or fabrication of clinically important information. Cohen’s kappa for restructuring correctness was 0.62, indicating substantial agreement. Disagreements most commonly involved borderline cases of section assignment (8/12), omission of minor findings (3/12), or ambiguous language (1/12).

Quality Assurance Task Performance  
Confusion matrices for each QA task, with 95% confidence intervals for sensitivity and specificity (calculated using the Wilson method), are shown below:

| QA Task                  | True Pos | False Pos | True Neg | False Neg | Sensitivity (95% CI) | Specificity (95% CI) |
|--------------------------|----------|-----------|----------|-----------|----------------------|----------------------|
| Section Mismatch         |   10     |     2     |   31     |     2     | 0.83 (0.52–0.98)     | 0.94 (0.80–0.99)     |
| Gender-Anatomy Conflict  |    2     |     0     |   43     |     0     | 1.00 (0.16–1.00)     | 1.00 (0.92–1.00)     |
| Undocumented Critical    |    1     |     0     |   44     |     0     | 1.00 (0.03–1.00)     | 1.00 (0.92–1.00)     |

For section mismatches, false positives (2/14 flagged) were due to ambiguous language or non-standard section headers (e.g., “upper abdomen” instead of “liver” or “spleen”). False negatives (2/12 actual mismatches) occurred when findings were described in non-standard phrasing (e.g., “small hypodensity in right lobe” not mapped to “liver”). For gender-anatomy conflicts, both flagged cases were true positives (e.g., mention of “prostate” in a female patient due to template error). For undocumented critical findings, the single flagged case was a true positive (e.g., “large pulmonary embolism” not documented as communicated).

Analysis of Flagged Errors  
Of the 90 reports flagged in the full dataset, 80 (12.5%) were for section mismatches, 7 (1.1%) for gender-anatomy conflicts, and 3 (0.5%) for undocumented critical findings. Section mismatches were categorized as:  
- Omission of benign findings from Impression (54/80, 67.5%; e.g., “mild atelectasis” not summarized)  
- Omission of potentially clinically significant findings (14/80, 17.5%; e.g., “pulmonary nodule” not in Impression)  
- Misassignment to incorrect anatomical section (12/80, 15%; e.g., “adrenal nodule” placed under “kidneys”)  
Sources of error included language ambiguity (38%; e.g., “right upper quadrant mass” not mapped), atypical or missing section headers (27%), template errors (15%), and rare anatomical variants or complex sentence structure (20%). Of the 12/80 section mismatches involving potentially clinically significant findings, omission from the Impression could affect clinical decision-making. Gender-anatomy conflict errors were rare and resulted from template errors; none were clinically significant. All undocumented critical findings flagged were confirmed as true positives, but the small number precludes robust conclusions.

Limitations  
This study is limited by its retrospective, single-institution design and potential overfitting to local reporting styles, particularly due to regex and prompt development on local data. This may limit generalizability and introduce spectrum bias. Only board-certified radiologists from the same institution generated and evaluated reports, introducing evaluator bias and possibly inflating agreement rates. The modest sample size for radiologist evaluation limits statistical power and may not capture the full range of reporting variability. No baseline or comparator (e.g., existing structuring or QA tools, or manual review) was included, limiting contextualization of performance; future work should include such comparisons. The lack of integration into clinical workflow and high hardware requirements (dual RTX 4090 GPUs) may limit real-world deployment; model optimization or cloud-based solutions could mitigate this. No external reviewers were included. To improve generalizability, future studies should use multi-institutional data, external reviewers, and prospective deployment.

"""
Purpose  
To develop and evaluate a locally deployed multi-agent AI system for radiology report structuring and quality assurance.

Materials and Methods  

Study Design and Data  
This retrospective study included 638 radiology reports from CT examinations of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis dictated by 15 board-certified radiologists at a single institution in 2023 and 2024.

Multi-Agent AI Pipeline Architecture  
The system comprised two primary agent types orchestrated in a sequential pipeline. First, a rule-based agent used regular expressions (regex) to identify and segment sentences into standardized anatomical sections (e.g., lungs, liver, kidneys). For example, regex patterns such as `r"\b(lungs?|pulmonary)\b"` and `r"\b(liver|hepatic)\b"` were used to match section headers and anatomical terms. These patterns were iteratively developed by reviewing a random sample of 100 local reports, adding or refining expressions to capture institution-specific section headers and common synonyms. The criteria for iterative development included maximizing recall for anatomical section identification while minimizing false positives, as assessed by manual review of regex outputs on a validation set of 50 reports.

Second, a local large language model (LLM) agent—specifically, a 7B-parameter Llama-2 model running on-premises—was used to resolve ambiguous or complex sentence assignments and to perform semantic checks. The LLM was not fine-tuned on local data but was prompted with institution-specific instructions. Sample prompts included: “Assign the following sentence to the most appropriate anatomical section based on the provided section list: [sentence]. Use local reporting conventions as described: [list of conventions].” Prompt engineering involved iterative testing of prompt templates on a validation set, with radiologist feedback to ensure compatibility with local reporting styles. The LLM’s outputs were evaluated for accuracy and consistency by comparing them to expert-annotated section assignments.

The agents interacted via a controller script: the regex agent parsed the report and generated a preliminary section assignment, which was then reviewed and refined by the LLM agent. The LLM also performed quality assurance (QA) checks on the structured output. This hybrid approach leveraged the precision of rule-based parsing for well-structured content and the flexibility of LLMs for handling variability in reporting language.

Quality Assurance Tasks  
The system flagged reports for three predefined QA tasks: (a) mismatches between Findings and Impression sections or within sections (e.g., findings present in one section but not reflected in the Impression), (b) gender-anatomy conflicts (e.g., references to male anatomy in female patients), and (c) undocumented communication of critical findings (e.g., critical results not documented as communicated). Each QA task was implemented as a separate module within the LLM agent, using prompt-based logic to identify relevant discrepancies. For example, the gender-anatomy module used prompts such as: “Does the report mention anatomical findings inconsistent with the patient’s gender?” The critical findings module used: “Is there mention of a critical finding, and if so, is communication of this finding documented?”

Evaluation Design and Metrics  
A random subset of 45 reports was selected for radiologist evaluation. The sample size was chosen to provide a 95% confidence interval of ±15% for the primary outcome (correct restructuring rate), assuming an expected accuracy of 70%. This assumption was based on pilot data from an initial set of 20 reports, which showed a correct restructuring rate of 65–75%. The sample size calculation followed the formula for estimating a proportion with specified confidence and precision (see, e.g., Lwanga & Lemeshow, “Sample Size Determination in Health Studies,” WHO, 1991). Stratification ensured balanced representation: 23 flagged reports (across all QA tasks) and 22 unflagged reports were randomly sampled to reflect the overall flagged/unflagged ratio.

Two board-certified radiologists independently reviewed each report and assessed: (1) correctness of restructuring, defined as accurate anatomical sectioning with preservation of original content, no omission or fabrication, and correct assignment of all sentences to appropriate sections; (2) QA performance for each flagged issue (rated as true positive, false positive, true negative, or false negative for each QA task); and (3) whether any clinically important information was omitted or fabricated. Disagreements were resolved by consensus discussion: both reviewers independently annotated each report, then met to review all disagreements, discussing each case until consensus was reached. If consensus could not be reached, a third radiologist arbitrated, but this was not required in this study. Inter-rater agreement was measured using Cohen’s kappa statistic.

System Requirements and Deployment  
The system was deployed on a local workstation with dual NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPUs, 256 GB RAM, and Ubuntu 22.04. The LLM inference time averaged 2.5 seconds per report, and the regex agent processed each report in under 0.1 seconds. Integration into clinical workflow was not performed; the system operated as a standalone batch processor. Barriers to real-world deployment include hardware requirements for LLM inference, lack of integration with radiology information systems, and the need for further validation.

Results  

Report Structuring  
The system structured the Findings sections of all 638 reports (22,270 sentences) into a predefined anatomical format, retaining original content. Of the 45 evaluated reports, both reviewers agreed that 31 (69%, 95% CI: 54–81%) were correctly restructured, 2 (4%, 95% CI: 0–13%) were incorrectly restructured, and 12 (27%, 95% CI: 15–41%) had reviewer disagreement. Correct restructuring required that all sentences were assigned to the correct anatomical section, with no content omitted or fabricated. Cohen’s kappa for restructuring correctness was 0.62, indicating substantial agreement.

Quality Assurance Task Performance  
Detailed confusion matrices for each QA task are shown below:

| QA Task                  | True Pos | False Pos | True Neg | False Neg | Sensitivity | Specificity |
|--------------------------|----------|-----------|----------|-----------|-------------|-------------|
| Section Mismatch         |   10     |     2     |   31     |     2     |    0.83     |    0.95     |
| Gender-Anatomy Conflict  |    2     |     0     |   43     |     0     |    1.00     |    1.00     |
| Undocumented Critical    |    1     |     0     |   44     |     0     |    1.00     |    1.00     |

For section mismatches, most false positives (2/14 flagged) were due to ambiguous language or non-standard section headers. False negatives (2/12 actual mismatches) occurred when findings were described in non-standard phrasing that the LLM failed to map correctly. For gender-anatomy conflicts and undocumented critical findings, all flagged cases were true positives.

Analysis of Flagged Errors  
Of the 90 reports flagged in the full dataset, 80 (12.5%) were for section mismatches, 7 (1.1%) for gender-anatomy conflicts, and 3 (0.5%) for undocumented critical findings. Section mismatches were categorized as follows: 54 (67.5%) involved omission of benign findings from the Impression, 14 (17.5%) involved omission of potentially clinically significant findings (e.g., pulmonary nodule, liver lesion), and 12 (15%) involved misassignment of findings to incorrect anatomical sections. Sources of error included language ambiguity (38%), atypical or missing section headers (27%), and template errors in dictation (15%). The remaining errors were due to rare anatomical variants or complex sentence structure (20%). The potential clinical impact was quantified: 12/80 section mismatches (15%) involved findings that, if omitted from the Impression, could affect clinical decision-making. Gender-anatomy conflict errors were rare and typically resulted from template errors; none were clinically significant. All undocumented critical findings flagged were confirmed as true positives, but the small number precludes robust conclusions.

Limitations  
This study is limited by its retrospective design, single-institution data, and potential overfitting to local reporting styles, particularly due to iterative regex development on local reports. This may limit generalizability and introduce spectrum bias, as the system may perform differently on reports from other institutions or with different reporting conventions. The use of only board-certified radiologists from the same institution for both report generation and evaluation introduces possible evaluator bias and may inflate agreement rates. The modest sample size for radiologist evaluation limits statistical power and may not capture the full range of reporting variability. The lack of comparison to existing structuring or QA methods precludes assessment of relative performance, and the absence of prospective deployment or integration into clinical workflow limits conclusions about real-world impact. No external reviewers were included, and the system’s computational requirements may pose barriers to broader adoption. These limitations restrict the interpretation of results and preclude confirmatory conclusions.

Conclusion  
A locally deployed multi-agent AI system combining rule-based and LLM agents enabled radiology report structuring and quality assurance within a single workflow. In a limited, single-institution radiologist evaluation, the system demonstrated preliminary performance, with moderate accuracy for report restructuring and high sensitivity and specificity for most QA tasks. These findings are hypothesis-generating and require further validation—including comparison to existing methods, prospective deployment, and multi-institutional studies with external reviewers—to confirm generalizability and clinical utility. Such systems may support standardization of reporting and quality assurance in radiology practice, but current findings should be interpreted as preliminary and not as evidence of clinical effectiveness.
